text: In the nineteen fifties, four sisters in central Mexico ran some of the most feared brothels in the country. People called them Las Poh-kee-ahn-chees.
text0: In the 1950s, four sisters in central Mexico ran some of the most feared brothels in the country. People called them Las Poquianchis.

text: Delfina, Carmen, Mah-ree-ah Loo-ee-sah and Mah-ree-ah de Heh-soos Gon-sah-lez Vah-len-sweh-lah grew up in Hah-lees-ko, daughters of a violent, hard-drinking small-town policeman.
text0: Delfina, Carmen, María Luisa and María de Jesús González Valenzuela grew up in Jalisco, daughters of a violent, hard-drinking small-town policeman.

text: When he shot a man, the family fled, changed its surname, and settled in Gwah-nah-hwah-toh.
text0: When he shot a man, the family fled, changed its surname, and settled in Guanajuato.

text: Delfina, the eldest, opened their first bar. A back room soon made more money than the bar itself. Before long, they ran brothels across Hah-lees-ko, Wanna-wahto, and Keh-reh-tah-ro.
text0: Delfina, the eldest, opened their first bar. A back room soon made more money than the bar itself. Before long, they ran brothels across Jalisco, Guanajuato, and Querétaro.

text: Their trap was simple: a newspaper ad. Housemaid wanted. Poor young women answered it… and never came home.
Inside, they were locked in, forced to work, and beaten. Debts they could never repay kept them there. Those who got sick, or became inconvenient, disappeared.
A former army captain, Delfina's partner, guarded the doors. And according to later accounts, some local officials looked the other way.
In nineteen sixty-four, a young woman named Kah-tah-lee-nah Or-teh-gah escaped, and reached the police in Leh-ohn.
text0: In 1964, a young woman named Catalina Ortega escaped, and reached the police in León.

text: Officers went to the sisters' ranch near San Francisco del Reen-cohn… and started digging.
text0: Officers went to the sisters' ranch near San Francisco del Rincón… and started digging.

text: Delfina and Mah-ree-ah de Heh-soos were arrested. Mah-ree-ah Loo-ee-sah fled at the last moment. The tabloid press splashed the story across Mexico.
text0: Delfina and María de Jesús were arrested. María Luisa fled at the last moment. The tabloid press splashed the story across Mexico.

text: Reports claimed ninety-one bodies: women, men, even unborn children. Historians still argue over the true number. Some say only eight victims were ever confirmed.
The surviving sisters were each sentenced to forty years in prison. Carmen had died of cancer years before.

Delfina died in prison in nineteen sixty-eight, in a strange accident. Mah-ree-ah Loo-ee-sah died behind bars in nineteen eighty-four. Mah-ree-ah de Heh-soos was eventually released… and vanished from public view.
text0: Delfina died in prison in 1968, in a strange accident. María Luisa died behind bars in 1984. María de Jesús was eventually released… and vanished from public view.

text: Mexico never stopped retelling the story: in Feh-lee-peh Kah-sahls' nineteen seventy-six film, in Hor-heh Ee-bar-gwen-goy-tee-ah's novel Las Muertas, and in a twenty twenty-five series.
text0: Mexico never stopped retelling the story: in Felipe Cazals' 1976 film, in Jorge Ibargüengoitia's novel Las Muertas, and in a 2025 series.

text: For more than a decade, everyone knew what those houses were. Nobody asked where the girls went. This is Plot Twist, with A. and R.
